clue.text: One who did not make a summer

definitions.text: One who did not make a summer

parts.words: One who did not make a summer
parts.note: the proverb says one swallow does not make a summer; here the swallow is one of the Swallows, the sailing children of Arthur Ransome's books, the eldest boy of the family

explanation.surface: A proverb about a single bird failing to bring on the warm season.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'one swallow does not make a summer' is turned on Arthur Ransome's Swallows and Amazons, where the crew of the dinghy Swallow are the Walker children; the eldest boy is one Swallow.
explanation.definitionFit: The captain of the Swallow in Ransome's children's novels is a single member of the Swallows, the proverb's lone bird.

clue.text: Exactly like Wallace's four men

explanation.surface: Something matches Edgar Wallace's quartet precisely.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means precisely, and is also the adjective in the title of Edgar Wallace's thriller The Four ___ Men about righteous vigilantes.

clue.text: Another pioneer of whodunits who, if "ex", one might yet dig up

definitions.text: who, if "ex", one might yet dig up

explanation.surface: An early detective-story writer whom one might one day disinter.
explanation.walkthrough: Fergus Hume wrote The Mystery of a Hansom Cab (1886), an early bestselling detective novel. Put EX in front of his name and you get a verb for digging up a buried body.
explanation.definitionFit: Fergus Hume was an early crime novelist, and his surname after the prefix ex- makes the word for disinterring a corpse.

clue.text: James's book about hunter and minor?

explanation.surface: A Henry James novel described as concerning a hunter and a youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: A hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged cover protecting the glass, and a minor in someone's legal care is their ward; Henry James's first novel bears the combined title.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's early novel has this title; a hunter is a type of pocket timepiece and a minor under guardianship is a ward.

clue.text: Unsuitable title, say, of feminist poet ()

indicators.note: 'say' signals that the title is spoken, matching the poet's surname in sound

parts.note: a lord is a nobleman's title, an unsuitable one for a feminist since it is male

explanation.surface: A male honorific is an odd label for a feminist writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty brackets in the printed clue probably held the poet's dates, lost in scanning. Audre Lorde was an American feminist poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Audre Lorde was an African-American writer celebrated for feminist and civil-rights verse.

clue.text: Hairpiece, say, possibly examined by Addison

indicators.note: 'say' tells the solver the hairpiece word is spoken, giving a party name of the same sound

explanation.surface: A wig, perhaps scrutinised by the essayist Joseph Addison.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Addison ran a periodical called The Whig Examiner in 1710, so a member of that party might be examined by him.
explanation.definitionFit: Addison's paper The Whig Examiner scrutinised the political party that opposed the Tories in eighteenth-century Britain.

clue.text: Former county of Wildfell Hall

explanation.surface: Asking which old shire contains Anne Brontë's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Huntingdon was the county town of Huntingdonshire, an English county abolished in 1974; Arthur Huntingdon is the dissolute husband in Anne Brontë's The Tenant of Wildfell Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The town names a defunct English shire, and is also the surname of the heroine's brutal husband in Anne Brontë's novel.

clue.text: Orangery, perhaps, of Mario Vargas Llosa ()

explanation.surface: A glass building for citrus trees attributed to the Peruvian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty brackets in the printed clue probably held a date lost in scanning. An orangery is a glass building for growing citrus; Vargas Llosa wrote the novel La casa verde, translated under this title.
explanation.definitionFit: An orangery is one example of a glazed plant house, and Vargas Llosa's 1966 novel is known in English by this name.

clue.text: Source of victory in the Louvre

definitions.text: Source of victory in the Louvre

parts.words: Source of victory in the Louvre
parts.note: the Winged Victory statue displayed in the Louvre was dug up on a Greek island in the northern Aegean, so the island is where this Victory came from

explanation.surface: A question about where triumph originates in the Paris museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victory' is not winning but Nike, the winged goddess statue on the Louvre's Daru staircase, named after the Greek island where it was found in 1863.
explanation.definitionFit: The Winged Victory sculpture was excavated on this Aegean island and is named after it.

clue.text: Gloomy dean, or one fora picnic?

explanation.surface: Either a pessimistic churchman or someone packing a hamper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fora' is the scan's run-together 'for a'. Dean W. R. Inge of St Paul's was nicknamed 'the Gloomy Dean'; William Inge, the American playwright, wrote Picnic (1953).
explanation.definitionFit: The pessimistic Dean of St Paul's and the American dramatist who wrote the play Picnic share this surname.

clue.text: Complete overshadowing of Christopher Hampton?

explanation.surface: Asking whether the playwright has been wholly put in the shade.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Hampton's play about Rimbaud and Verlaine has this title; read plainly, it is the sun or moon entirely blotted out.
explanation.definitionFit: A full astronomical blotting-out of sun or moon is complete overshadowing, and Hampton's 1967 play bears that title.

clue.text: Big Bang recorded by Larkin

explanation.surface: Philip Larkin captured the origin of the universe.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Larkin's poem about a mining disaster bears this title, the last poem in High Windows.
explanation.definitionFit: A big bang is a blast, and Larkin's poem about a pit disaster is titled with that word preceded by the article.

clue.text: Mercenary card game from Germany

explanation.surface: A hired soldier and a game of cards, both originating in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is the French form of German Landsknecht, a hired foot soldier of the Renaissance, and also a card-gambling game named after them; 'from Germany' links both senses to their origin.
explanation.definitionFit: A German soldier of fortune of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries gave his name to a gambling game played with cards.

clue.text: Quite unmoved by Typhoon?

parts.note: plainly, resistant to tempest; the capital T points to Joseph Conrad's novella Typhoon, so it also suggests a reader untouched by the book

explanation.surface: Someone left entirely indifferent by Joseph Conrad's sea story.
explanation.walkthrough: Typhoon is a Joseph Conrad novella, so 'unmoved by Typhoon' looks like a literary judgement; read as weather, it describes something built to withstand gales.
explanation.definitionFit: Something able to withstand tempests is not shifted by a violent tropical cyclone.

clue.text: Sort of lord Prufrock felt he was

definitions.text: Sort of lord Prufrock felt he was

parts.words: Sort of lord Prufrock felt he was
parts.note: in Eliot's poem Prufrock says he is not Prince Hamlet but one who will do to swell a progress, a minor courtier of that kind

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of nobleman Eliot's timid speaker saw himself as.
explanation.walkthrough: In T. S. Eliot's The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock: 'No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be; / Am an attendant lord'.
explanation.definitionFit: Prufrock calls himself a lord in waiting, a hanger-on serving a prince rather than the hero.

clue.text: Ode to Arms rearranged for sports arena

indicators.note: 'rearranged' says the letters of the poem title are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A poem's title is reshuffled to name a stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rearranged' shuffles the nine letters of ODE TO ARMS into a domed stadium's name; the Houston Astrodome was the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Houston stadium was the first domed sports venue, and its name became a general term for one.

clue.text: Half of Angus Wilson's attitudes

parts.note: Angus Wilson's 1956 novel is titled with a hyphenated two-part adjective before Attitudes; the first half of that adjective is wanted

explanation.surface: A claim that the novelist holds only part of his opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: Angus Wilson's novel Anglo-Saxon Attitudes takes its title from Lewis Carroll; the first part of the hyphenated word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The first element of the hyphenated English-Germanic adjective in Wilson's title is a prefix meaning English.

clue.text: Insectivore domesticated by Petruchio ()

explanation.surface: A small bug-eating animal tamed by Shakespeare's suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Petruchio woos and tames Katherina in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew; the word also names a tiny insect-eating mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: The small mouse-like mammal feeds on insects, and it is Katherina's label in the comedy where Petruchio tames her.

clue.text: Were those of Margaret Kennedy replicated?

definitions.text: Were those of Margaret Kennedy replicated?

parts.words: Were those of Margaret Kennedy replicated?
parts.note: Margaret Kennedy's 1957 novel names its champions as being of Clone, and a clone is a copy, so the question asks whether those figures were copied

explanation.surface: A question whether a novelist's characters were duplicated.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Kennedy wrote The Heroes of Clone; 'replicated' plays on clone. The grid as scanned reads THEHEEOES, a misprint for the real title words.
explanation.definitionFit: The first two words of Kennedy's title The Heroes of Clone name the champions who belong to Clone, a copy.

clue.text: Success is the one sin against our fellows " (Ambrose Bierce)

definitions.text: Success is the one sin against our fellows " (Ambrose Bierce)

parts.words: Success is the one sin against our fellows " (Ambrose Bierce)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Bierce's line has a missing adjective before sin, meaning beyond forgiveness

explanation.surface: A cynical aphorism from The Devil's Dictionary about envy of achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Ambrose Bierce: 'Success is the one unpardonable sin against our fellows'. The missing word, which the scan lost along with the opening quotation mark, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bierce calls success the sin that cannot be forgiven, the adjective for beyond excusing.

clue.text: "Iso tragic, the house rose like magic" (W. F. Hargreaves)

definitions.text: "Iso tragic, the house rose like magic" (W. F. Hargreaves)

parts.words: "Iso tragic, the house rose like magic" (W. F. Hargreaves)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation; the scan runs the pronoun into the following word and drops the missing verb, meaning performed on stage

explanation.surface: A music-hall line about a performance so tragic the audience stood up.
explanation.walkthrough: From W. F. Hargreaves's music-hall song The Night I Appeared as Macbeth: 'I acted so tragic the house rose like magic'. The scan shows 'Iso' where the gap after 'I' was lost.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the past tense of the verb for performing a part on stage, which the comic actor of the song did badly.

clue.text: Gala locally staged featuring French composer

indicators.note: 'featuring' says the composer's name appears within the words gala locally, so the run is hidden there

explanation.surface: A local gala puts on a show of a French composer's music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staged featuring' points to the run spanning gaLA LOcally; Édouard Lalo wrote the Symphonie espagnole.
explanation.definitionFit: Édouard Lalo was a nineteenth-century French composer, best known for his violin concerto Symphonie espagnole.

clue.text: A high time for Fred Zinnemann

definitions.text: A high time for Fred Zinnemann

parts.words: A high time for Fred Zinnemann
parts.note: Zinnemann directed the 1952 western High ..., so a 'high' time of day is twelve o'clock in his film's title

explanation.surface: The film director enjoying a celebratory occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A high time' looks like a celebration; it is the midday hour that follows 'High' in Zinnemann's western High Noon.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is the time in the title of Zinnemann's western, when the sun is highest.

clue.text: Instrument superseded by its transposed version

definitions.text: Instrument superseded by its transposed version

parts.words: Instrument superseded by its transposed version
parts.note: the early keyboard named loud-soft was replaced by the modern one named soft-loud, the two halves of its name swapped round

explanation.surface: An instrument made obsolete by a version in a different key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transposed' looks musical, changing key; here it means the two halves of the name are swapped, giving the modern piano's full name, which displaced the earlier instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century early piano was displaced by the modern keyboard whose name puts the same two Italian words in the other order.

clue.text: Eliot's Hayslope patriarch with presidential connections?

explanation.surface: An old villager from George Eliot's novel linked to the White House.
explanation.walkthrough: Hayslope is the village of George Eliot's Adam Bede, where old Taft is the aged patriarch; William Howard Taft was the 27th US president.
explanation.definitionFit: The elderly villager in Adam Bede shares a surname with a US president of 1909 to 1913.

clue.text: Stupid officiousness of Bumble, for example

definitions.text: Stupid officiousness of Bumble, for example

parts.words: Stupid officiousness of Bumble, for example
parts.note: Mr Bumble in Oliver Twist is a pompous parish officer, and the clue asks for the state or character of such officers

explanation.surface: Describing a bumbling person's pointless fussiness.
explanation.walkthrough: Bumble looks like a verb for clumsiness; it is Mr Bumble, the parish beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist, whose petty pomposity gave beadledom its meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty bureaucratic pomposity is the quality typical of a parish officer such as Mr Bumble in Dickens.
